articles.title: Why McKinstry leader Matt Allen is betting on clean nuclear, geothermal and smarter buildings
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Matt Allen wasn’t sure he wanted to pursue a career at McKinstry , the Seattle-based company his grandfather co-founded in 1960. The business started with plumbing and piping, evolving into a construction and energy services firm with national reach.
But after joining in 2012, Allen began appreciating the impact McKinstry has helping customers find affordable, planet-friendly solutions for their operations.

It could be as simple as replacing an old, natural gas boiler with a high-efficiency heat pump, Allen said, “but you feel like you’re part of that customer’s journey, and our societal journey, to get to a carbon-free environment.”
Now serving as McKinstry’s chief client officer, Allen shared his thoughts with GeekWire about sustainability. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.
What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

With all the expansion in energy consumption and the race for compute, I worry about maintaining our progress around decarbonization. And having a young son, I do worry about rising temperatures and what the world is going to look like for young people. However, I am encouraged to see a continued emphasis in decarbonization action across industries. On the data center side, the hyperscalers that we work with are evolving their designs to focus on sustainability as much as possible.

Human ingenuity has been able to innovate our way through challenging spots. Western Washington is a big hotbed for clean nuclear solutions, deep geothermal, and some of these new, emerging clean energy generation technologies. When enough brain power is focused on those pieces, combined with capital infusion, progress is made. I think there is a lot of motivation to increase clean energy generation through innovative solutions. That gives me hope.
If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

Clean nuclear fusion. If you could accelerate Helion, Zap or Avalanche, that would be great. Or deep geothermal — Fervo Energy, for example, is developing a commercial project down in Utah. If we could snap our fingers and get some of those technologies to market, you could rapidly accelerate people’s willingness to electrify systems and connect to a clean grid. A lot of this comes back to having a clean grid, so when we’re doing electrification projects at a building level, the building owners can have confidence in having energy availability to reduce their carbon footprint.
What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Operations — that’s a big focus for us, finding optimized ways to operate buildings and turn down systems when appropriate. We joke that everyone talks about first cost when they’re building or doing a retrofit, but they don’t talk about the ongoing operation and maintenance costs. If we can find more efficient ways to operate buildings, that reduces strain on the grid and reduces overall energy consumption while providing real savings for our clients.

We rigorously track greenhouse gas emissions. Our baseline started in 2019, around the time we signed the Amazon Climate Pledge, which has a net zero target of 2040. We hope to hit net zero sooner. We’re also tracking a couple of different measures. One is GHG emissions on a per-revenue basis. So, as we’re growing our revenue, are we still taking a bite out of emissions? We also track it on a per-FTE-employee basis. Those two measures hold us accountable as an institution to make sure we’re not taking our eye off the ball moving toward net zero.
The scope of the climate challenge is daunting — how do you approach this work?

For the work we do for customers, or even the work we do internally to reduce our own carbon footprint in our business operations, you just take it quarter by quarter, project by project — focus on doing a good job for your customers, bring things in on time and on budget, and help strategize with them on the most cost-effective ways to do things.

We do the same thing internally, creating a glide pattern. There is no magic bullet, so you take it one piece at a time. A good example for us is our biggest carbon emitter — our vehicle fleet. We have 600 service vans and another 300 utility trucks out on the road, and we track our progress toward electrifying that fleet. We’re 10 or 15% of the way through, and every time a vehicle needs to be replaced, we replace it with an electric one.
What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

I just hope that there isn’t an existential climate crisis, that we’ve taken collective action — whether it’s the Paris Climate Accord or some other macro commitment — and come together as a society to ensure we’ve left the campsite in a better place than we found it and that our world remains a habitable, thriving, healthy environment for the next generation to live in.

articles.title: Strauss Proposes Program Phasing Out Street Parking for RVs
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: At the public safety committee meeting on August 11, Seattle Councilmember Dan Strauss introduced a legislation package that he said would help people who are currently living in their recreational vehicles (RVs). However, while the package includes funds for services such as safe lots and RV storage, it also introduces a RV permit program aimed at removing all RVs on Seattle’s streets – a move that advocates say could leave RV residents worse off.

In Seattle, people can currently park their RVs overnight in industrial areas or, according to posted signage, up to 72 hours in one place, like other vehicles. However, the new legislation would change the law so that RVs could only park for two hours in one place, and would be forbidden from parking anywhere overnight (from midnight to 6am). Failure to follow these laws could result in towing without notice.

The only exception to this new rule would be for people living in RVs and “fifth wheel” trailers who succeeded in applying for a special permit during a one-time census. In order to receive a permit, residents would have to agree to receive services and ultimately move into other housing or shelter. There would be one permit per person who would have to prove they were the registered owner of the vehicle.

In order to retain a permit, residents would have to abide by a number of regulations , including having the vehicle display a license plate and vehicle identification number, not leaving trash around, not hosting a group of five or more people, not leaving a pet tied up unattended, etc.
Permit holders would be able to turn down up to six offers of shelter or housing, but after that, they would lose their permit.
Strauss framed his plan as a way to help people who live in their vehicles.

“Today, we have zero places for people who live in their vehicles to come inside to. We have no city systems or city teams that are designed to help people that are experiencing homelessness with vehicles,” Strauss told The Urbanist . “We need to create those systems, and from there as well, RVs are a unique type of vehicle that are not built for year-round habitation.”

The legislation package consists of five ordinances and a resolution. In addition to the permitting program, the ordinances would update outdoor storage land use codes, expand the Finance and Administrative Services (FAS) Director’s authority to execute various related leases, clarify and add two new criteria to the definition of a “junk vehicle,” and allocate $5 million of funding.

The resolution states the intent to move the ecoblocks that have multiplied in industrial areas popular for RV parking, such as Ballard, SODO, and West Seattle, within six months of implementation of the program. However, it doesn’t specify who holds responsibility for ensuring this removal takes place, which can be a costly endeavor and requires somewhere else to store the heavy blocks.

The proposed funding for Strauss’s program would consist of $1.5 million in one-time dollars and $3.5 million in ongoing funds. Part of the money would be used to pay for eight new positions: seven new outreach counselor positions within the Human Services Department (HSD) and one new permit technician within the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). As written, the legislation gives SDOT the task of establishing program standards and administrative procedures for the permitting program.
Alison Eisinger, the executive director of the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, questioned the plan to hire new outreach workers as part of the overall strategy.

“Seven or eight full-time city employees suggests a disproportionate investment in coordination of inadequate resources, as opposed to an investment in adding good resources that will help get more people where they need to go,” Eisinger said.

The Unified Care Team – the interdepartmental team that performs the City’s homelessness outreach and sweeps – has tallied 145 vehicles that meet the permitting program’s definition, Strauss said, adding he believes this is an undercount.

In addition to the safe lot – Glassyard Commons – opening in West Seattle in November, Strauss’s plan calls for a second safe lot. Assuming the second lot is the same size, that could mean 150 parking spaces for RVs. But Strauss said he wants to collaborate with service providers to decide whether the second safe lot should prioritize RVs.

Seattle Public Utilities (SPU) already runs an RV Wastewater Program in order to mitigate RV wastewater spill incidents, in partnership with St. Vincent de Paul. Every quarter. the team performs an average of 300-400 wastewater pump-outs.

“Before the program was launched, spill incidents peaked at 117 in 2019,” an SPU spokesperson told The Urbanist . “In its first year, the program reduced spills by 60%, and incidents have continued to decline in both frequency and severity. Today, spill incidents average about 10 per year and our estimates show the program saved about $300,000 in cleanup costs in 2025 through this proactive spill reduction work.”
Strauss was clear with The Urbanist that he ultimately wants to remove RVs from Seattle’s streets.

“We want to create a program that serves humans, that centers humans, and we're at a point where RVs are not an appropriate type of vehicle to be on our streets anymore here in our city,” Strauss said. “I think of it like a boat. You know, people have boats, and they can either park them in their driveway, which is off of a city street or they can store it, in the same way that an RV can be parked in your driveway or it can be stored.”

The analogy is an interesting one since boats are generally considered to be luxury consumer goods while unhoused people living in their RVs often have few resources and fewer choices. Houseless RV owners rarely own land on which to store their RV, hence the dilemma.
Strauss also said the permitting program would only address people living in RVs and travel trailers.

“If they are in a place in their life where they're choosing living in a vehicle, [that] is a better option than anything else, there's nothing in this legislation that outlaws, bans, or penalizes living in a vehicle. We are saying we're not going to allow RVs on the street anymore, which means somebody could live in a 15-passenger van. They could live in their truck, a truck with a camper on it,” Strauss said. “If you want to own a different type of vehicle, you have that ability.”
“The people I know who've lived in RVs, that's been the best option available. Period. It's not about choosing one RV over another or one vehicle over another,” Eisinger told The Urbanist .

Graham Pruss, the executive director of the National Vehicle Residency Coalition, used to be the only outreach worker for people living in vehicles in Seattle between 2013 and 2015, with a caseload of around 1,500 people. Pruss said people living in their vehicles saw it as a more stable option to the alternative, one that provided privacy, a place to store their belongings, and sometimes even a way to build a kind of property equity, all while maintaining a connection with their community.

“The folks that were living in vehicles often described a much deeper level of stability, a deeper level of connection,” Pruss said. “They often had bills that they had to pay, maintenance for their vehicle. They had to keep their driver's license, their insurance. They often keep it operable. At the very least, they saw this vehicle as an important piece of property.”
While advocates are pleased about the idea of more services, they are concerned at the punitive nature of the RV permitting program.

“How does this permit proposal fit into our landscape of housing and shelter? It doesn't. The permit, the way that it's currently constructed, it would be punitive and not helpful to move people into shelter or housing,” Hali Willis, the community policy manager of the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, told The Urbanist . “We like to support efforts that are based in evidence and facts and will accomplish the goals of helping people achieve stability and live well, and we don't believe that this permitting proposal will get us there.”
A similar program in San Francisco led to more than five times the number of RVs towed versus households placed into housing through their permit program.

“I think the biggest impact we would see almost immediately is you would see more people living outside and not in vehicles,” said G.B., a volunteer with Stop the Sweeps. “This doesn't solve anything.”

G.B. called out the difficulty people living in their vehicles would have trouble filling out the necessary paperwork to apply for a permit, how they might not have proof of ownership of the RV in which they’re living, and how they might be displaced from their communities in order to take a spot in a safe lot. G.B. also called out the high price the City would be paying for towing contracts to enforce the new parking laws.

“It could be very sensible to focus on the most positive and generally broadly agreed to proposals, namely a safe parking lot, the ability to understand more about people who are living in their RVs in the city of Seattle, and this idea of potentially storing people's vehicles if the fact that they don't have anywhere to park long term could be a barrier to them being able to accept shelter or housing,” Eisinger said. “But we have also told Councilmember Strauss that we believe that it is desirable and reasonable for him to defer this idea of a complex, hard to implement, bureaucratic, and expensive permitting process that is unlikely to actually improve upon people's living circumstances, and he has articulated a willingness to continue the conversation.”
Jay from Stop the Sweeps said that the services provided by the new legislative package might not be worth the punitive measures.

“It really feels like this is completely aligned with the standard thinking of the strategic approach to addressing homelessness, which is that every carrot must have a stick,” Jay said. “We can't just roll out additional services. They must be accompanied by punishment, and in this case in particular, I think that the carrot is hardly worth the stick.”

Pruss explained that for many, housing is not only unaffordable but also inaccessible, citing the difficulties faced in obtaining housing by people impacted by the criminal legal system, undocumented immigrants, young adults just aging out of the foster care system, and more.

“This is the private property, legal, valuable asset of people who are using this to survive the housing crisis that we all see around us – the lack of emergency shelters, the lack of permanent supportive housing – it simply does not exist,” Pruss said. “And to put in further regulations does not solve that problem.”
Pruss was also concerned that the legislation would move authority to SDOT, a move that he’s seen cause trouble in Californian cities like San Jose and Oakland.

“The redesignation of the vehicle from a homeless management encampment response to the Department of Transportation takes away many of the protections of homeless management responses, and it essentially says this is now an object that is designated as an obstruction that can be removed and destroyed with very little due process, almost as though it's like just a crashed vehicle on the side of the road,” Pruss said.
During the discussion of the legislation at the public safety committee earlier this month, Councilmember Bob Kettle expressed his negative opinion of people living in RVs.

“From the public safety perspective, as pretty much everybody knows, once you have five RVs together, one's going to start dealing drugs. Once you have a drug market, you have a stolen goods market,” Kettle said. “There's a clear public safety nexus.”

“I would question the research behind that,” Pruss said. “I have been to RV parking programs that are officially run. I'm the former strategic advisor on homelessness to the city of San Jose, the third largest city on the West Coast. We ran safe and supportive parking programs with well over 50 RVs in them, and that was not the case. There was never a report of anything like that, and I have never seen research that would suggest otherwise.”

According to the legislation as written, the deadline for the City to develop the RV permitting program and begin the new parking restrictions would be April 30 of next year, with enforcement beginning by July 31.

articles.title: What to know about voting in Washington amid federal tumult
articles.author: Paris Jackson
paras: Washington State Secretary of State Steve Hobbs shares important election reminders ahead of November. He’s also fighting to protect our state’s decades-old vote-by-mail system amid attacks on it by the President.
In the first installment of a 5-part series, we cut through voting disinformation to better arm you before hitting the ballot box.
Washington’s August Primary is over; the next big voting cycle is the general election.

While most state election information is common knowledge, there still may be some confusion. We want to help you get up to speed with crucial new information, such as changes to postmarking a ballot.
We tapped the state’s top election administrator, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, to ask two questions to get the facts about the state’s election system.
The first question: Is it still okay to vote by mail in Washington in the upcoming November 3rd election?

“Absolutely. But if you're about a week from the election, you should put it in a drop box, not a mailbox, because the USPS, they had some rulemaking about a year ago on when the postmark is made,” Hobbs said.

Hobbs says ballots have to be postmarked before 8 p.m. on that Tuesday. He says if you insist on wanting to mail your ballot or use the US Postal Service, the best thing to do, especially within that week, is to go directly to a postal clerk.
The second question: How secure are elections in all 39 counties in Washington?

“Very secure. And in fact, if you have any doubts, go visit your local elections center, contact your county auditor. Or if you're in King County Elections Director, they would love to have you in there [office] and actually see the elections go on. For with your own eyes, you can actually see the ballots going out, coming in, being opened. I highly encourage that,” he said.
All this week, we’ll have more from state officials about what you need to know about elections in the state.

Amateur sleuths and armchair psychologists have been creating content throughout the several weeks of the trial, pointing out perceived discrepancies in evidence. articles.title: ‘It’s absolutely criminal’: US tipping culture has reached the UK – and is causing chaos
articles.author: Emine Saner
paras: Service charges used to be a matter of choice, but now consumers feel obliged to pay them for even a cup of coffee. How do we navigate this minefield and who is really profiting?

In a London pub, Greg Double was brutally confronted with the reality of Britain’s evolving tipping culture. “I was annoyed about the pint being eight quid, but then when you put service on top, it’s absolutely criminal,” he says. In the past, you might have told the bar staff to keep the change or have a “drink” on you, but since when did we routinely tip in pubs? Or coffee shops? Or, worst of all, at self-service machines? Tip creep is happening.

Tipping was awkward enough in the UK when the general rule was 10% at a restaurant, plus anxiety about whether you should tip the hairdresser, babysitter or food-delivery driver. Now, with tipping suggested ever more frequently, US-style, it has become a minefield to Britons. The amounts edge higher – in fancier London restaurants, a 15% service charge is relatively commonplace. And it’s often asked for – in coffee shops for example, when you pay – before any service is delivered.

articles.title: ‘A bit like meditation’: why Saw is my feelgood movie
articles.author: Emma Madden
paras: The latest in our series of writers picking their go-to comfort films is a grimy and gory trip back to the start of a surprisingly uplifting torture porn franchise

I was petsitting recently for a white suburban family, with the typical streaming habits therein. They had two kids; their most-watched shows, according to the history that showed up on the screen, were Bluey for the kids and The Office for the adults. When they came home from their weeklong trip, they would’ve found their watch history upheaved. The Bingos and Michael Scotts all erased by Saw I, Saw II, Saw III, Saw IV, Saw V, Saw VI, Saw 3D, Saw Spiral, Saw Jigsaw and, finally, my new favourite, Saw X.

I was obsessed with the Saw franchise well before I ever saw it. At 11, as Jigsaw puppets became Halloween costumes, I went to bed each night convinced Jigsaw was going to scoop me up in a van because the word “hell”a popped into my head. By 13, I looked up every film on Wikipedia and read through each trap with terrified excitement. By 14, I drank my first can of Stella and typed Saw II into YouTube, watching it in 12 installments. It was utterly horrifying. And so, so, so much fun.

articles.title: Betrayal by Luke Harding review – could Donald Trump be a Russian asset?
articles.author: Lawrence Freedman
paras: A Guardian correspondent’s sobering account of the US betrayal of Ukraine – and the possible reasons behind it

American presidents have struggled to get the measure of Vladimir Putin. When George W Bush met him in 2001, he reported that he had “looked the man in the eye”, got a “sense of his soul” and found him “trustworthy”. Barack Obama thought Putin was making a mistake with his interventions in Ukraine and Syria, but didn’t do much about it. Joe Biden backed Ukraine’s resistance to the Russian invasion, yet his fear that Putin would reach for the nuclear button if backed into a corner made him risk averse. He worried about the impact of the sort of long-range strikes against Russian territory that Kyiv is now launching on a daily basis.

This caution frustrated Ukrainians to the point that they looked forward to Donald Trump shaking things up after he won re-election. Be careful what you wish for: the returning president thought his rapport with Putin would be enough to get Russia to sign up to an immediate ceasefire. In Trump’s head it was President Zelenskyy, fighting a war he was bound to lose, who was the problem.

articles.title: Many Americans are moving away from congregations, but not necessarily from religion – movies, plays, art and social media fill the gap
articles.author:
<name>Laura Yares, Assistant Professor of Religious Studies, Michigan State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/laura-yares-592333"/>
paras: “Emma,” a young Jewish woman who we met in 2019, didn’t belong to a synagogue. She didn’t have a Jewish partner. She didn’t observe Jewish rituals regularly. On most surveys about religion, she would not seem very engaged with Judaism.

But as Emma talked about what she did in her free time, a very different picture began to emerge. She visited Jewish websites and enjoyed listening to Jewish music. She read books about Jewish topics and had recently attended a retreat for young Jewish adults to learn Torah while also doing yoga.
She was highly invested in learning about Judaism, but she explored her identity without joining traditional institutions.

Most major surveys about religion ask whether someone belongs to a congregation, how often they attend services , whether they pray regularly and whether belief is important in their lives. Those measures help identify broad shifts, like the growing percentage of Americans who are religiously unaffiliated : the “nones.”

But many Americans’ religious lives, like Emma’s, are not disappearing; they are moving away from membership of traditional institutions . To understand what religion looks like in 21st-century America, researchers may need to ask different questions.

As scholars of Judaism and education , we have been exploring how people learn about religion beyond traditional places like synagogues, Jewish schools and summer camps. Between 2019 and early 2023, we spoke with hundreds of people and explored different leisure time activities to discover what people learn about Judaism and Jewishness through cultural arts.

We interviewed dozens of audience members at Jewish-themed shows on Broadway, such as “Leopoldstadt” and “Parade.” We attended Jewish concerts and asked attendees what they learned. We explored how social media communities offer spaces to talk about different Jewish topics, like what fans learned about ultra-Orthodox Judaism from watching the television show “Shtisel .”

Our research revealed that there is a vibrant ecosystem of people learning about religion in their leisure time. Through the arts, both Jews and non-Jews encounter Jewish history, Jewish religious practices and representations of Jewish communities.
Most people we spoke with told us that they felt meaningful connections to Judaism during activities that would rarely appear on a standard religion survey.

“Joan,” an unmarried woman in her 50s from Connecticut, told us that she was deeply invested in Judaism, but felt that synagogues and Jewish community centers were not welcoming to single people without families. Instead of joining a Jewish institution, she watched Jewish-themed TV shows and movies on Netflix, and joined social media communities to chat with other fans.

“Luis,” who lived in Boston but was born in Argentina, was a Sephardic Jew , a group that traces their ancestry and traditions to Jewish communities who once lived in Spain and Portugal. His wife was Ashkenazi, meaning her ancestors came from Central and Eastern Europe . She considered herself secular, and so the couple joined the Worker’s Circle , a nonreligious Ashkenazi institution rather than a synagogue.
Yet Luis loved deepening his knowledge of Sephardic culture, and he often attended concerts of music in Ladino, a Sephardic language related to Spanish , with other Sephardic immigrants.

For Joan and Luis, these activities were not peripheral to their Jewish lives. Rather, they were central avenues for learning and community . We interviewed hundreds of Jews who told us that cultural experiences were opportunities to reflect on Jewish practices, explore questions of belonging, connect with family histories and find friends with common interests.

Some aspects of these patterns were distinctive to Judaism. Historically, many Jews have understood Judaism to be a cultural world , and not only a theological tradition. Learning about cultural dimensions of Judaism has long been part of Jewish education .

The broader phenomenon of informal learning, though, extended far beyond a single tradition. Across America, increasing numbers of people learn about religion through media, cultural productions and digital networks. Christians may study biblical themes through podcasts, online discussion groups or religious influencers . Muslims may participate in online learning communities that connect believers across the world.

The challenge for religion researchers, then, is not simply to determine whether engagement with religion is rising or falling. Rather, it is to develop more nuanced ways of understanding how people explore religious themes and practices, beyond traditional institutions . Only then can we more fully understand how contemporary Americans actually live their religious lives.

articles.title: Most Westerners know Buddhism through meditation, but everyday Buddhist life looks quite different in Thai temples
articles.author:
<name>Brooke Schedneck, Associate Professor of Religious Studies, Rhodes College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/brooke-schedneck-681711"/>
paras: I recently returned from leading an educational program in Thailand focusing on how Buddhists practice the religion in their day-to-day lives. The participants – Buddhist practitioners from North America and Europe – wanted to deepen their understanding and practice of the religion.
Many Western Buddhists’ practices centers on meditation. As a scholar of contemporary Thai Buddhism , I have taught many students and adults in the U.S. who have a similar understanding.

Although meditation can be very important to many practitioners, as I show in my 2023 book, “ Living Theravada ,” Buddhism is more than an intellectual tradition focused on the mind. In countries with a majority Buddhist population, such as Thailand, Buddhist practice involves rituals, offerings to monks and visits to temples, among others traditions.
Here are three ways in which Buddhism shapes daily life in Thailand.

A central part of daily practice is performing rituals associated with merit-making. To make merit means to do something morally good that will generate good karma – actions that are believed to impact this life and future ones. The simplest way to do this is to make a monetary donation to a temple.

There are often several merit-making activities in temples that are meant to be fun and engage participants. For example, one can place a small sheet of gold leaf on a part of a Buddha statue where one would like help or healing, such as one’s mouth if someone often uses their voice for their work or the ankle where they would like help or healing.

Another fun activity is ritually purifying the “chedi,” or a large monument that enshrines sacred relics. Thai Buddhists fill a container with blessed water, which is attached to a pulley that leads to the upper part of the chedi. The container empties when it reaches the top, and participants make merit by symbolically cleansing the sacred monument.

Making offerings to specific Buddha statues representing the different zodiac signs based on one’s day and year of birth is common. In Thai temples, one can often find eight Buddha statues in a row, all in different poses; each represents a day of the week, with Wednesday being divided into morning and evening. Those born on a Friday, for example, will make an offering to the Buddha statue corresponding to their day of birth.

Worshipers can also make merit by directing donations to the zodiac animal associated with their birth year. Those born during the year of the monkey can place a flag or paper decorated with the monkey symbol on or around a sacred structure inside the temple hall. In other words, individuals can make merit connected to their own circumstances, relationships and aspirations, while practicing generosity.

A foundational feature of Theravada Buddhism is the relationship between monastics and the lay people. This relationship is a delicate balance where laity offer alms while the monks offer spiritual wisdom and guidance. As monks’ lives are dedicated to Buddhism, they are believed to accrue much merit, which Buddhists believe they can then transfer to people who make offerings.

However, there are times when these bonds can be tested. During COVID-19, for example, the laity did not go into the temples for fear of contracting the virus. This made it difficult for monks to obtain food and maintain connections with their local Buddhist community.

The laity’s faith in monks and in their ability to provide merit and moral guidance can suffer if monks break their vows, such as by drinking alcohol or having sex. In 2022, for example, a well-known monk was found to have had an affair with a model. Thai Buddhists felt disappointed and raised questions about the ability of young monks to take their vow of celibacy seriously.

The ultimate goal of Buddhist practitioners is enlightenment, or nirvana – freedom from the cycle of birth and death and suffering. But most Buddhists see this goal as out of reach in this lifetime and instead have desires for worldly things , such as getting a job, winning the lottery or finding a spouse.

Thai Buddhist temples often have icons of Hindu gods, such as Ganesha and Brahma , who are believed to grant these worldly wishes. Some temples may also have shrines dedicated to indigenous gods or spirits of the land. Since these gods are believed to be concerned with worldly success, they are popular places where people pray for wealth, job promotion, romance or fertility.

These rituals involve an exchange, where worshipers promise to return with certain objects the god or spirit is believed to enjoy, such as hard-boiled eggs, figurines of elephants or flower garlands, if their wish comes true.

Buddhism in Thailand is embedded into everyday lives and collective concerns. At the end of 10 days, my program participants learned the value of merit-making and felt benefit from performing rituals. They saw how Buddhism extends beyond the individual pursuit of mental transformation through meditation.

articles.title: Fish DNA in Ozark streams reveals region’s complex geologic history
articles.author:
<name>David Duvernell, Professor of Biological Sciences, Missouri University of Science and Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/david-duvernell-2754314"/>
paras: My students and I encountered a mystery. We were partnering with the Missouri Department of Conservation to monitor for fish presence and abundance in the Missouri Ozarks. We visited half a dozen rivers and streams across the region and collected a few cups of water from each.

We were testing for DNA in the environment to determine which species had left behind their genetic material and were therefore present in the stream . There was no need to capture or even see the species themselves. We were delighted to detect a variety of species in their appropriate habitats that are considered at risk in Missouri , including the lake sturgeon , crystal darter and Alabama shad . In the surface waters emerging from one large underground spring, we detected DNA from a cave-dwelling fish species that would never have been detected by researchers who caught or looked only for fish in the surface waters.

But there was a problem: We were certain we would find one particular species in every stream: the bleeding shiner ( Luxilus zonatus ), one of the most common fish in Ozark streams. To have confidence in our results we needed to understand why the bleeding shiner DNA did not show up in every sample, as we had expected. We checked our sampling technique, our water chemistry and other aspects of our testing.

In the data itself, we found a clue: The streams in which we detected bleeding shiner DNA all drained to the southern Ozarks, and the streams in which bleeding shiner DNA was not detected were all in the northern Ozarks. We could draw a line through the north-south drainage divide between those areas.

Some follow-up sleuthing revealed something we hadn’t known at the start: Northern Ozark bleeding shiners have a different DNA history from their southern relatives, even though the fish look identical and are, in fact, the same scientific species.

To human observers, the Ozarks can seem a relatively continuous landscape. For fishes, however, that landscape is divided into a series of separate drainage networks. Streams may arise only a few miles apart yet flow in opposite directions, ultimately connecting to entirely different river systems with distinct geologic histories.

Hundreds of thousands of years ago, the ancestors of northern populations interbred with another species of shiner, leaving behind a genetic signature of ancient hybridization that survives today, but only in certain drainages. Though they look the same, and were in rivers humans view as neighboring, these fish had distinctly different genetic histories.

We had been looking for just one DNA signature, assuming that all bleeding shiners would share that identity. Environmental DNA analyses like this can sometimes turn up unknown or unidentifiable sequences of DNA . When we looked more closely at those results, we were able to identify which previously unknown sequence corresponded to the northern populations of bleeding shiner.

Our findings were a concrete illustration that today’s rivers are products of ancient landscapes. During the glacial advances of the Pleistocene epoch – from about 2.5 million to about 12,000 years ago – some rivers repeatedly changed course.

Streams that are isolated today were once connected. Others that share a common geography and are ecologically quite similar today may have had entirely separate histories. The species that exist in rivers and streams today are the products of those long and complicated geological and evolutionary processes .

Specifically in Ozark streams, northern drainages that flow into the Missouri and Mississippi rivers were directly influenced by glacial advances that molded, modified, wiped out and recreated drainage connections and patterns of flow across the landscape.

In contrast, the southern Ozarks drainages were relatively isolated from disruptive glacial advances. South-flowing drainages, such as the St. Francis, Black, White and Spring rivers, contain more endemic species and genetically unique populations. Examples include the genetically distinct Black River walleye and numerous minnows, sunfishes and darter species that are unique to specific streams.
This project reminded my students and me that biodiversity monitoring by sampling DNA in the environment doesn’t just reveal what species are present.

The water samples we took contained records of the ancient landscapes that shaped those species. Every sample of river water is more than an inventory of life – it’s a window into the evolutionary history of an entire watershed.
David Duvernell receives funding from Missouri Department of Conservation.

articles.title: How do ice cubes cool a drink?
articles.author:
<name>Matthew Koss, Professor of Physics, College of the Holy Cross</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/matthew-koss-2701293"/>
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com .
How do ice cubes cool a drink? – Helen, age 12, Boston, Massachusetts

I like to make my own iced tea. First, I steep about a quart of terrifically strong hot tea and pour it into a pitcher loosely filled with ice cubes straight from the freezer. The result is about two quarts of delicious, cold tea, with a few ice cubes floating on top.

What’s the science behind my perfect pitcher of iced tea? A simple answer is that the near-boiling tea transferred its hotness to the below-freezing ice cubes. This transfer raised the temperature of the ice cubes so that much of the ice melted. That both cooled the tea to a refreshing drinking temperature and diluted it for a proper taste.
My iced tea process reminds me of physics experiments I worked on that flew on the space shuttle Columbia in the 1990s. I was interested in how liquids turn into solids in the absence of gravity.

Both those space experiments and the making of iced tea depend on liquids or solids getting hotter or colder in just the right combination. The explanation for how it all works depends on two related concepts: temperature and energy.

The concept of temperature grew out of the sense of what feels hot and cold to human touch. Boiling water is too hot to touch safely, and a candle flame is even hotter. Ice cubes feel cold. A thermometer is a special hotness meter that more reliably and repeatably determines the degree of hotness or coldness of substances than our sense of touch.

Eighteenth-century physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit defined the point when ice melts or water freezes as 32 degrees of temperature – what we we now call 32 degrees Fahrenheit in his honor. He also defined the temperature at which water boils and turns into steam to be 212 degrees F.

Energy is a more complicated concept. One way to think about energy is as a way to track what it costs nature to makes changes from one set of conditions to another. There are many types of energy. Thermal energy is related to temperature. Kinetic energy is based on how fast stuff is moving. Other forms of energy include, to name only a few, electromagnetic energy, chemical energy and nuclear energy.

Another type of energy is called potential energy and it accounts for the energy stored by the forces acting between or within objects. It is those forces that control the transfers from one type of energy to another. Examples of potential energy that you can see are a rubber band stretched and about to snap back or a boulder sitting at the top of an incline, ready to roll. On a microscopic level, potential energy is composed of all the interacting forces between the atoms and molecules that make matter.

Once a boulder begins to roll down the hill, its potential energy from the force of gravity first transforms to kinetic energy and then maybe to thermal energy or to the work of knocking down a tree. Although energy can transform from one type to another, the total amount of energy always remains the same. Whatever amount of energy is gained in one place must be lost from somewhere else. Scientists call this rule of nature conservation of energy , or in cases involving thermal energy, the first law of thermodynamics .

As an example of the distinction between energy and temperature, compare a cup of hot tea and an iceberg. The hot tea is clearly at a much higher temperature than the iceberg, but the large iceberg has vastly more energy than the tiny cup of tea.

The tea is hotter than the iceberg because the molecules that make up the tea are moving faster than the molecules that make up the iceberg. The temperature is essentially the average energy of the molecular movements.

The speed and energy of a typical single liquid molecule are greater than for a typical single iceberg molecule. But the iceberg has many, many more molecules, all moving around, interacting with each other and transferring vast amounts of energy between their kinetic and potential energies .

Back to the question of making iced tea. When the hot tea encounters the ice cubes, the molecules of tea-flavored water collide with the molecules on the surface of the ice. The liquid’s molecules slow down. The ice’s molecules speed up, and some even leave the solid and mix in with the liquid tea.
The tea loses thermal energy and lowers its temperature. That energy transfers to the ice, which gains that energy and increases its temperature.

The process of energy moving from one place to another due to differences in temperature is called heat transfer. Left to itself, nature transfers thermal energy only from higher to lower temperatures. That observation is called the second law of thermodynamics . It’s why you will never see a cup of cold tea turn into a cup of ice cubes and hot tea.

In my pitcher, this process continues until the ice eventually reaches a temperature of 32 degrees F, its melting temperature. At that point, the ice cannot take any more energy and stay solid, even though it is still absorbing thermal energy from the hotter tea. Instead, any additional thermal energy absorbed by the 32 degrees F ice transforms it into 32 degrees F water.

Heat transfer cooling means that energy leaves the tea. Conservation of energy means a matching amount of energy raises the temperature of the ice to 32 degrees F and then turns some of that ice into 32 degrees F water. Thus the thermal energy of the tea turns into the potential energy of the water molecules that used to be part of the ice, lowering the temperature of the liquid in the pitcher. The process continues until eventually all the tea and whatever ice that survived the melting are at the same refreshing 32 degrees F.

Keep all this in mind as you enjoy your ice-cold drink on a hot summer day. Don’t dawdle, though, as the air temperature in the room or your warm hand on the glass can transfer their thermal energy to melt the rest of the ice and then begin to raise the temperature of your drink!

articles.title: Just as the world appears to be losing its appetite for books, William T. Vollmann pens a 3,000-page novel
articles.author:
<name>Christopher Coffman, Master Lecturer in Humanities, Boston University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christopher-coffman-2741569"/>
paras: With forecasters of doom debating the end of reading , of publishing and of literacy in general , what should we make of William T. Vollmann’s forthcoming novel, “ A Table for Fortune ”?
Spanning four volumes at 3,000 pages, is it madness? A determined attempt to silence print’s naysayers?
I have been writing about Vollmann’s works since I penned the introduction to “ William T. Vollmann: A Critical Companion ” more than 10 years ago.
The 67-year-old author has spent his career going big, in every sense, and I would not be the first to describe his approach to his art as uncompromising .

His projects grapple with weighty matters such as global poverty , the history of North America and climate change . Few of his roughly 25 books run under 500 pages. About half try to keep his readers engaged for several hundred beyond that. Many of them supplement the text with photographs, epigraphs, glossaries, family trees, sketches, timelines, variant tables of contents, alternating fonts and notes to the reader. The essay “ Rising Up and Rising Down ,” his philosophical and journalistic inquiry into the nature of violence, clocks in at over 3,000 pages across seven volumes.

But to those who might argue that this is the worst time to put a monster of a novel into print since the days before Johannes Gutenberg created the movable-type printing press in the 15th century, I would say that Vollmann’s approach is needed now more than ever.

After reading Vollmann’s works and occasionally speaking with him in person or via post, I join others in being powerfully struck by his unrivaled intelligence, empathy and work ethic. His books are not big for the sake of being big. They reflect the deep sense of responsibility he feels toward his subjects.

In the case of “A Table for Fortune,” that subject is, as Vollmann declares in the opening volume, the cause and effects of 9/11 – “tracing the roots of that crime in one direction and its poisoned harvest in another.”

It is a novel of ideas and a novel of feelings, the former expressed in the tale of a CIA man who bears the code name DAVE, and the latter the purview of his son, Matthew. DAVE is a brilliant, deeply committed Cold War analyst whose faith in America’s mission gradually erodes after 9/11 and the ensuing war on terror . Matthew, by contrast, is less interested in geopolitics but just as invested in questions about the nature of America. His desire for purpose in life is deeply informed by a notion that the nation still harbors opportunities for freedom. At the same time, his search for that freedom leads him into such dangers as homelessness and addiction.
The book will be published at a challenging moment for Vollmann — and for reading more broadly.

In 2022 alone, he lost his daughter, was dropped by Viking , his longtime publisher, and the supporters of his archives at Ohio State, and got hit by a car while crossing a street. He has also been fighting an incurable case of colon cancer, racing against the clock to see a few final projects to completion.

Meanwhile, the nation’s educational system is constantly having to calibrate its expectations for reading down , and publishers find themselves confronting steadily worsening odds that the average reader will even pick up a book in the next year.

To the extent that there is a reading public, they’re assumed to be increasingly ill-equipped to handle the very sorts of things that motivated Viking to drop Vollmann : His books seem too long, too complex and too expensive to publish.

But I think the apparent gulf between Vollmann’s work and America’s dismal reading data could be thought of differently. What if the challenging complexity and political engagement of his tomes are exactly what’s needed?

Today, fact and fantasy intermingle freely as a consequence of political scheming and jockeying for economic advantage. Political discourse is reduced to opinions at once homogenous and balkanized , reinforced by the echo chambers of the day’s regnant algorithms . Then there are the fragmented attention spans birthed by our dearly beloved screens, which cultivate a kind of cognitive whiplash that vacillates between amnesia and yearning for more .
It’s easy to become dispirited and cynical: The field seems too big, and the game rewrites the rules too quickly for anyone to figure out how to overcome these forces.

What happens, Vollmann’s works ask, when serving the good is revealed as its opposite? What happens when the response to the horror of 9/11 becomes an arena for perpetration of further crimes, rather than the healing of wounds already inflicted?

Even as the invasion of Afghanistan in 2001 and of Iraq in 2003 became largely condoned by the American public, displacement, suffering and impasse persist in the region, now in the form of the ongoing conflicts in the Gaza Strip and Iran. The broader post-9/11 strategy seems directed against stable governance in the Middle East generally.

Whether one works for the CIA – as do several of Vollmann’s central characters in “A Table for Fortune” – or occupies a less central node in the networks of power, it is not hard to recognize that the best intentions can be perverted, that one’s idealistic labor may unknowingly be lent to furthering the cloaked ambitions of the wicked.

Such legacies of 9/11 are the sort of uncomfortable and powerful matters to which Vollmann directs attention. And if people are to grapple with such thorny topics, they need to be delineated in detail and at length, as they are in “A Table for Fortune.”

A work like this is not only a book about powerful conspirators. It is also a book that can help keep people afloat as they navigate the tumultuous seas of the post-truth era, dodge the whirlpools of digital banality and resist the leviathans of techno-capitalism.
Vollmann is not going it alone. Far from it.

He follows the tradition of what scholars call “ literary maximalism ” – works that are ambitious in scale and scope, containing narratives flush with surprising intersections, proliferations and divergences.

His works build on such earlier mega-novels as Thomas Pynchon’s “ Gravity’s Rainbow ,” William Gaddis’ “ The Recognitions ” and John Barth’s “ The Sot-Weed Factor ,” which together confront the complexities of America’s past and present. Their topics include the limits of authenticity and how to grasp understanding in a world awash in deceit.
Vollmann also joins ambitious contemporaries such as David Foster Wallace, whose “ Infinite Jest ” interrogates the loss of self to entertainment and the vapid slogans of popular culture.
Behind each is arguably the grandest American novel of all, “ Moby-Dick .”

I was not surprised to learn that Vollmann visited Polynesia in 2019 to walk in Herman Melville’s footsteps. Melville, after all, was wracked by difficulties that should never have been his to bear: constant problems with publishers, uncomprehending reviews, endlessly faltering finances and the loss of a teenage son to a self-inflicted gunshot wound that may not have been an accident.
In other words, Vollmann’s work is not entirely an outlier. Neither is his readership.

Indie publishing houses like Deep Vellum are celebrating thick books, and not just those from American authors. Mircea Cărtărescu’s 2015 “Solenoid,” which begins with a fictional biography set in Cold War Romania, has earned a dedicated following in translation. Michael Lentz’s “Schattenfroh,” a 1,001-page novel that follows the internal narrative of a tortured subject confronting centuries of history, likewise garnered considerable attention when its English translation dropped in 2025.

In his note to the reader, Vollmann explains that the ongoing failures most strikingly signaled by 9/11 are matters of “lessons not learned,” “expediencies of power” and “consciences disabled,” in addition to that most cunning arbiter: “chance.”

The same list of conditions is relevant to the debates about our faltering literacy. If, as seems likely, “A Table for Fortune” is one of Vollmann’s final books, it crowns a career that reminds readers that the world’s troubles must be apprehended as much more complex than a few data points and alarmist sound bites suggest.
Indeed, books like “A Table for Fortune” may be among the most essential tools for keeping our heads above water.

articles.title: Etzioni on AI: An Opinionated Glossary of AI
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: Jargon stinks. What do the terms open weights, RAG, and agent mean exactly? Here’s a plain English, slightly snarky glossary of befuddling AI terminology with references for further reading.

AI is a broad name for the technology. Machine learning is the part where a system learns from data instead of following rules somebody wrote, a neural network is the structure that does the learning, and deep learning just means a neural network with a lot of layers.
Here’s the nitty-gritty: the terms that get used loosely, and the distinctions the loose usage hides.
ChatGPT is the app you open; an LLM, or large language model, is the AI running inside it.
“Frontier” isn’t a technical category at all. It means the handful of biggest and most capable models at any given moment, so the trophy keeps changing hands.
Everyone says “LLM” and hardly anyone could define it on the spot. “Frontier model” is worse. It’s a ranking, announced by the people being ranked.
Further reading: How ChatGPT Works: A Non-Technical Primer (MIT Sloan). Rama Ramakrishnan walks through the predict-the-next-word mechanism everything else is built on.

A prompt is the thought, question, or instructions you provide to the LLM (plus whatever the app added before it without telling you). The LLM takes the prompt and generates words, both in its internal “thinking” process and in the answer it shows you.
Tokens are (roughly) the words going in and coming out. The model chops your prompt into tokens, then produces more of them as it answers, and they’re what the industry charges by.

Parameters, also called weights, are the numbers inside the model. A frontier model has hundreds of billions of them and the biggest now run to trillions, and nobody can tell you what any single one does.
Parameter counts get quoted like horsepower. The number nobody advertises is how many tokens it takes to answer your question, and that’s the one that shows up on the bill.
Further reading: The only AI glossary you’ll need this year (TechCrunch, July 2026). Its entries on tokens and weights are the clearest short treatment of the building blocks.

Pre-training is feeding the model most of the internet, so it learns to predict the next word in a sentence. That’s the expensive part, and it produces something that knows a great deal but can’t follow an instruction.
Post-training is where people rank its answers and it learns to give more of what ranked well. Fine-tuning is post-training done by you, to somebody else’s model, on your data.
Pre-training costs hundreds of millions and gets you a model that won’t answer a question well. Post-training is what gets you the product.
Further reading: Illustrating Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Hugging Face, 2022). The clearest walk-through of how ranking a model’s answers becomes a signal for training.

From scratch, you buy (or rent) the computers and do the work to build and train a model. Distillation trains a cheap model on an expensive model’s outputs, so it inherits the behavior without the bill. Distillation is against most AI companies’ terms of service.

OpenAI accused DeepSeek of distilling its models, which is a bold position for a company that trained on the whole internet without asking. Learning from other people’s work is fine right up until the other people are you.
Further reading: OpenAI accuses DeepSeek of “free-riding” on American R&D (Rest of World, February 2026). OpenAI’s memo to Congress, and an analyst’s reply that no model is an island.
Training is how you build a model. Inference is what happens every time it answers: the model runs and produces a result.

Training is a one-time cost. Inference is a cost you’ll pay forever. Training runs for months and costs hundreds of millions; one inference, meaning one answer, costs a fraction of a cent, and it happens billions of times a day.
Training costs get announced. Inference costs get discovered. Only one of them shows up in a press release.
Further reading: Why AI’s next phase will likely demand more computational power, not less (Deloitte, 2025). Inference reaches about two-thirds of all AI compute in 2026, up from a third in 2023.

We typically use LLMs by accessing an app like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini. But experts often want the model itself, not just an app wrapped around it. Open weights means that an AI expert can download the model and run it on a server. You don’t get the data or the code that made it.
Open source means data and software that experts can use and modify, which almost no major model offers (AI2’s Olmo is a rare exception).

API-only means you can’t have the model at all. You send your text to the company’s computers, the answer comes back, and you pay for every use, which is also what’s happening when you use ChatGPT or Claude through an ordinary account.
Open weights is how you claim the open-source mantle without giving much away. Open washing, basically.

Further reading: Open-Weight Models Aren’t Enough. We Need Truly Open Source AI Models for Science and Society. (Stanford HAI, August 2026). James Landay’s term for downloadable weights without the data or code is “open distribution.”
The context window is how much text the model can hold in mind at once, including your question and everything pasted into the conversation.
Memory is a feature that saves facts about you and slips them back into the context window later.
RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation, searches a document collection and drops the relevant passages into the context window before the model answers.
Nothing in the model remembers you. The app keeps a file on you and pastes it in before every conversation, and that’s a less charming way to describe the same feature.

Further reading: Glossary of Terms: Generative AI Basics (MIT Sloan Teaching & Learning Technologies). Defines context window and RAG in plain language, and is careful to put the model’s “memory” in quotation marks.

A chatbot answers and stops. A workflow runs the steps you defined, in your order. An agent receives a goal instead of steps, and works out for itself what to do, calling out to other software and checking the results until it’s done or stuck.
Ask about a delayed flight and a chatbot quotes you the policy; a workflow uploads the refund form you built; an agent rebooks you.
Useful test: if it decides its own next step, it’s an agent. If you decided the steps, it’s a workflow.
Further reading: Building effective agents (Anthropic, December 2024). The source of the distinction: workflows run predefined code paths, agents direct their own.

A hallucination is a confident falsehood, like a citation to a paper that doesn’t exist. The model isn’t lying; it has no notion of truth to violate. It’s producing text that looks like the right kind of answer.
AI slop is a different failure: accurate, fluent, and worthless. Think of the LinkedIn post that says nothing in 300 fluent words.
AI cream is the third case and the rare one: superb writing authored with the help of AI.

articles.title: Sound Transit Says Train Derailment Was Isolated Incident
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: After a snag-free stretch setting ridership records during the World Cup, Sound Transit has had a few big service hiccups in the past month and a half, with a derailment on August 1 topping the list.

A roof hatch issue on July 9 also caused a major service disruption that lasted 15 hours, after the malfunctioning hatch took out an overhead wire between the University of Washington and U District stations.

"Mechanical issues disrupted trains on July 10th and again on July 20th , when brakes on a train wouldn’t release ," Seattle Transit Blog's Sherwin Lee recounted . "Then the following day on July 21st, a power outage resulted in a temporary suspension of service between Beacon Hill and Tukwila International Blvd stations."
However, the agency has said that overall service reliability is trending up, and emphasized they have no reason to expect the derailment or roof hatch issue to repeat.

The derailment on Saturday, August 1 happened at low speed in the Chinatown-International District (CID) station just before midnight. It caused no injuries, as the train was not yet in service and empty, other than the operator.

The derailment did, however, shut down light rail service in the downtown tunnel until 2:15pm Sunday, August 2. A full restoration of service waited while Sound Transit investigated the incident. During the disruption, Sound Transit truncated service, operating a bus bridge to replace the shuttered downtown tunnel.

Because no crossover tracks exist within the downtown tunnel, any blockage or system disruption within the tunnel typically shuts the entire downtown section from SoDo to Capitol Hill. Sound Transit has raised the idea of adding crossover tracks, but the proposal remains unfunded and yet to be queued up. Such crossover tracks would allow Sound Transit more service pattern options in the tunnel, such as bypassing a particular platform or set of platforms in emergencies or maintenance situations.
Public information about what caused the derailment was scant, other than a paywalled Seattle Times article from Mike Lindblom on Sunday morning.

King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci, who serves as one of 18 members of the Sound Transit Board of Directors, brought up the issue at the Rider Experience and Operations (REO) Committee on August 6.

"On the derailment, can I just say it's been a few days: I think we should have some more information about the cause, to be honest, because a derailment is a life-threatening situation," Balducci said. "So, I'm really interested to know that we know what happened so that it's not going to happen with a train with people on it. That's very concerning."

At Balducci's prodding, Sound Transit CEO Dow Constantine expanded on the brief summary of the derailment in his CEO report to start the meeting, which treated the incident as handled and in the rearview mirror.

"This is a section of the track that veers off and goes into a pocket track," Constantine said. "So, that is a track that is not for passengers between the north and south tracks in the International District Station. As this non-passenger train was being repositioned from the south end in order to add capacity there."
Sound Transit had been storing extra trains at the station to help handle traffic leaving the Ed Sheeran concert at Lumen Field.

"[The train] was taken onto that side track, and this is where we know the two bolts sheared off bolts that were holding that curved track that goes to the pocket track. We don't know why they sheared off, however, and so Ed [Cobean], could you talk a little bit about the investigation that's being done on those two bolts, and then on the other fasteners that are similar, and there are few of them in the rest of the system."
Ed Cobean, Sound Transit's Deputy CEO, Chief Transit Operations, pointed to steps the agency was taking to prevent another derailment on pocket tracks.

"There is only one other switch in our system – this is special track work – that has anything that resembles it." Cobean said. "So, we've already done a full inspection on the other switch. Have put the existing switch bolts back into place. It's been repaired. We are also sending those bolts out for metallurgy testing to see if they can come back to us [with improvements]. We do know that it was the original construction, original bolts from when that was built 20 years ago, and we are going to do additional testing and inspections across the entire system for other switches, not just these two alone."

The Urbanist reached out to Sound Transit this week to see how the investigation was progressing into how the bolts were sheared off without the agency's track inspection team noticing, but no new details were offered.

"We have confirmed that the shearing of the two bolts caused the track to become misaligned, resulting in the derailment," Sound Transit spokesperson Henry Bendon said in an email. "The incident occurred on a section of special track work that is unique in our system to access the pocket track at International District/Chinatown Station - although it is used in many other systems. That track was inspected, repaired, and returned to service the next day, and we have no reason to believe this will happen again."

At the REO Committee, Balducci did bring up that rider communication could have been better during the unexpected outage, noting many had reached out to her to share their confusion when the downtown tunnel closed unexpectedly.

"I just wanted to share that I personally got a whole bunch of feedback about wayfinding in the aftermath of a major unplanned disruption like that," Balducci said. "People not knowing how to get to the shuttles, and so I would love to hear some more here today, if possible, about what happened and sort of how we can upgrade our standards for making sure we have immediate announcements of delays, how long they're going to be, if we know what the cause is, and then how to get to a shuttle easily."
Constantine did acknowledge some room for improvement on that front.

"We are quite rigorous in our processing of lessons learned," Constantine said. "And we are continuing to build the agency's capacity for continuous improvement, so that each time we have something that arises that's unusual, we can learn from it, and we can make the experience better for our passengers. And this is certainly one of those events where we have opportunities to learn more and improve."
Derailments are very rare in Sound Transit's system. Lindblom reported the incident earlier this month was only the second known derailment that disrupted passenger trips since service began in 2009.

Another incident on August 10 in Rainier Beach was initially reported on social media as a derailment, but turned out to be a track switch issue that did not result in a derailment. The issue led to a comparatively short service disruption while the switch was investigated.

Sound Transit does periodically run staff through simulations to prepare them for emergency situations, including derailments. Andrea Trepadean, Chief Safety Officer at Sound Transit, described such training exercises at a REO Committee meeting in December.

"We do emergency preparedness drills and exercises, and part of those drills and exercises we do simulate self evacuation of passengers," Trepadean said at the time. "When we have those drills and exercise and there is a self evacuation, what we're focused on is the communication and the recovery of the scene and the safety of the passengers. Referencing the event on Sunday where the Sounder passengers self evacuated, the safety of the passengers was the conductor's focus. The conductor immediately pivoted to protect those passengers by making sure we had all train traffic stopped and the tracks were protected with a track block, and we had personnel activated responding to assist with a large-scale self evacuation of passengers."
Sound Transit simulated a derailment as part of preparation to launch the Federal Way Link Extension in December.

"We recently did an exercise on our Federal Way Link Extension," Trepadean said in December. "It was a full-scale exercise that we performed on October 25 and this was part of that simulation. The first responders involved in that exercise knew the general theme of the exercise, which was a simulated train derailment."

Of course, running a simulation or two does not always mean that the agency's entire apparatus is ready to seamlessly pick up the slack when a derailment happens... say near midnight on Saturday with droves of Ed Sheeran fans emptying out of a stadium to find the light rail station is suddenly shut down.

One theory for the spate of outages is that the agency was pushing the system so hard (including temporarily suspending its monthly maintenance program to squeeze out more capacity) during a ridership-heavy month buoyed by the local World Cup matches that maintenance issues piled up. According to the agency, World Cup traffic wear and tear did not relate to any of the recent service disruptions.
A draft agency service plan does look at expanding maintenance windows across the light rail network by shortening service spans at certain times.

"To your questions about maintenance windows, we are currently in the early stages of developing the 2027 service plan, and are seeking public feedback on the possibility of additional time for maintenance," Bendon said. "This would build on the success we’ve been seeing with our monthly maintenance program, but is entirely unrelated to your question about World Cup ridership."
